title: 07. Concurrency: Synchronous vs Asynchronous vs Multithreading vs Multiprocessing
summary: You take Order from Table 1 → You go to kitchen → You STAND THERE AND WAIT until food is ready → You bring food → Then go to Table 2.

sections.title: Explanation (Like You're a Junior Developer)
sections.body:
Imagine you are a **waiter in a restaurant**.

**🔴 Synchronous (Blocking) — The Bad Waiter**

You take Order from Table 1 → You go to kitchen → You **STAND THERE AND WAIT** until food is ready → You bring food → Then go to Table 2.

While you wait at the kitchen, no other table gets served. This is **Synchronous** — do one thing, wait for it to finish, then do next thing.

```
Table 1 ──[order]──[WAIT WAIT WAIT]──[serve]──▶
Table 2                                          ──[order]──[WAIT]──[serve]──▶
Table 3                                                                        ──...
TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶
```

**🟢 Asynchronous (Non-Blocking) — The Smart Waiter**

You take Order from Table 1 → Tell kitchen → **Go take order from Table 2** → Tell kitchen → **Go check Table 3** → Kitchen calls you → Bring food to Table 1 → Kitchen calls again → Bring food to Table 2.

You never stand idle. While kitchen prepares (I/O waiting), you do other work. This is **Asynchronous** — start a task, don't wait, do other things, come back when task signals it's done.

```
Table 1 ──[order]───────────────────────[serve]──▶
Table 2        ──[order]──────────[serve]──▶
Table 3               ──[order]──[serve]──▶
TIME ──────────────────────────────────────▶  (MUCH FASTER!)
```

**🔵 Multithreading — Multiple Waiters (Same Kitchen)**

You hire 3 waiters. Each waiter handles one table at a time. They **share** the same kitchen (memory). Good for I/O tasks but Python has **GIL** (Global Interpreter Lock) which prevents true parallel execution of Python bytecode.

**🟣 Multiprocessing — Multiple Restaurants**

You open 3 completely separate restaurants. Each has its own kitchen (memory). True parallelism. Good for **CPU-heavy** tasks like image processing, ML training.

sections.title: When to Use What?
sections.body:
| Scenario | Best Choice |
|---|---|
| Waiting for network calls (API, DB) | ✅ **Async** |
| Reading/Writing many files | ✅ **Async** |
| CPU-heavy computation (ML, math) | ✅ **Multiprocessing** |
| Legacy sync libraries, simple parallel | ✅ **Multithreading** |
| Simple sequential scripts | ✅ **Synchronous** |

sections.title: 5 Examples
sections.body:
**Example 1 — Synchronous (Slow, Sequential)**
```python
import time

def fetch_user(user_id):
    print(f"Fetching user {user_id}...")
    time.sleep(2)  # Simulates a DB/API call — BLOCKS everything
    print(f"Got user {user_id}")
    return {"id": user_id, "name": f"User_{user_id}"}

def main():
    start = time.time()

    fetch_user(1)  # Wait 2 seconds
    fetch_user(2)  # Wait 2 more seconds
    fetch_user(3)  # Wait 2 more seconds

    print(f"Total time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~6 seconds

main()
# Output:
# Fetching user 1...
# Got user 1
# Fetching user 2...
# Got user 2
# Fetching user 3...
# Got user 3
# Total time: 6.00s
```

**Example 2 — Asynchronous (Fast, Concurrent)**
```python
import asyncio
import time

async def fetch_user(user_id):
    print(f"Fetching user {user_id}...")
    await asyncio.sleep(2)  # Non-blocking wait — gives control back to event loop
    print(f"Got user {user_id}")
    return {"id": user_id, "name": f"User_{user_id}"}

async def main():
    start = time.time()

    # All 3 run CONCURRENTLY
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_user(1),
        fetch_user(2),
        fetch_user(3)
    )

    print(f"Total time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~2 seconds!
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
# Output:
# Fetching user 1...
# Fetching user 2...
# Fetching user 3...
# Got user 1
# Got user 2
# Got user 3
# Total time: 2.00s  ← ALL 3 done in 2 seconds instead of 6!
```

**Example 3 — Multithreading (I/O Bound)**
```python
import threading
import time

def fetch_data(source):
    print(f"[Thread] Fetching from {source}")
    time.sleep(2)  # Blocking, but thread yields during I/O
    print(f"[Thread] Done with {source}")

start = time.time()
threads = []

for source in ["Database", "API", "Cache"]:
    t = threading.Thread(target=fetch_data, args=(source,))
    threads.append(t)
    t.start()

for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(f"Total: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~2 seconds
# BUT: threads share memory → risk of race conditions
```

**Example 4 — Multiprocessing (CPU Bound)**
```python
import multiprocessing
import time

def heavy_computation(n):
    """CPU-intensive task — computing sum of squares"""
    result = sum(i * i for i in range(n))
    print(f"Process: computed sum for n={n}, result={result}")
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    start = time.time()

    with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=3) as pool:
        results = pool.map(heavy_computation, [10_000_000, 10_000_000, 10_000_000])

    print(f"Results: {results}")
    print(f"Total: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # True parallelism — uses multiple CPU cores
```

**Example 5 — Visualizing the Difference Clearly**
```python
import asyncio
import time

# ─── Synchronous version ───
def sync_download(url):
    time.sleep(1)  # pretend downloading
    return f"Data from {url}"

def sync_main():
    urls = ["url1.com", "url2.com", "url3.com", "url4.com", "url5.com"]
    start = time.time()
    results = [sync_download(url) for url in urls]
    print(f"[SYNC]  Time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~5 seconds
    return results

# ─── Asynchronous version ───
async def async_download(url):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # pretend downloading (non-blocking)
    return f"Data from {url}"

async def async_main():
    urls = ["url1.com", "url2.com", "url3.com", "url4.com", "url5.com"]
    start = time.time()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*[async_download(url) for url in urls])
    print(f"[ASYNC] Time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")  # ~1 second
    return results

# Run both
sync_main()
asyncio.run(async_main())

# Output:
# [SYNC]  Time: 5.00s
# [ASYNC] Time: 1.00s  ← 5x faster for I/O-bound!
```

How it relates to async: asyncio is actually unaffected by the GIL positively — since asyncio is single-threaded by design, it never needs to compete with the GIL.
